statement: In the United States, benzodiazepines were named on the death certificate in 21.0% of opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from 8.7% in 1999 and after a peak of 26.2% in 2010; in 2015–2017 the share was 21.7% of 122,940 deaths: about one in three deaths involving prescription opioids (33.3%) or methadone (32.4%), about one in six involving heroin (15.9%) or synthetic opioids such as fentanyl (17.4%), and 26.9% of women's against 19.2% of men's deaths. Death certificates under-record drugs (12% of drug poisoning deaths in 2017 had no specific drug named) and testing varies between states and years, so these shares are probably too low. In the records of people who had opioid prescriptions, larger shares of deaths happened while a benzodiazepine was prescribed: 1,185 of 2,400 overdose deaths (49%) among US veterans on opioid painkillers in 2004–2009, and 971 of 1,256 accidental opioid-related deaths (77.3%) among Ontario public-drug-plan opioid recipients in 1997–2013, against 56.4% of matched living controls. These shares describe how often the drugs occur together in deaths; on their own they do not show how much benzodiazepines add to the risk of dying.
plain: How often are benzos involved in opioid overdose deaths? On US death certificates, benzos were listed in about 21 of every 100 opioid overdose deaths in 2017, up from about 9 in 100 in 1999. They were listed more often when the opioid was a prescription opioid or methadone (about 1 in 3 deaths) than with heroin or fentanyl (about 1 in 6), and more often in women's deaths than in men's. Death certificates miss some drugs, so the real numbers are probably higher. In studies of people with opioid prescriptions, half of the overdose deaths among US veterans, and three in four accidental opioid deaths in Ontario, Canada, happened while a benzo was also prescribed. These numbers show how often the drugs appear together in deaths, not how much benzos add to the risk.
population: People who died of opioid overdose: all US death certificates 1999–2017 (399,230 deaths; 122,940 in 2015–2017); US veterans on opioid analgesics who died of drug overdose, 2004–2009 (2,400); Ontario public-drug-plan opioid recipients who died an accidental opioid-related death, 1997–2013 (1,256)
exposure: Benzodiazepine named on the death certificate (ICD-10 T42.4), or prescribed at the time of death (veterans: current prescription; Ontario: dispensed in the 120 days before death)
comparator: None for risk (shares among deaths); for context, matched living opioid recipients in Ontario
outcome: Share of opioid overdose deaths involving benzodiazepines, by year, opioid type and sex
magnitude: US death certificates (Tori et al., 2020): benzodiazepine co-involvement in all opioid overdose deaths 8.7% (1999), 26.2% (2010), 21.0% (2017); 2015–2017: 26,728 of 122,940 (21.7%), men 19.2%, women 26.9%; heroin 15.9% of 43,940, methadone 32.4% of 9,868, prescription opioids 33.3% of 41,709, synthetic opioids 17.4% of 57,459 (subtypes overlap); by state 5.4% to 45.5% (median 22.0%). Death rates for opioid overdoses involving benzodiazepines rose 10.3-fold from 1999 to 2017, against 5.0-fold for all opioid overdose deaths. Prescription records: US veterans on opioid analgesics, 1,185 of 2,400 overdose deaths (49%) during current benzodiazepine prescription (Park et al., 2015); Ontario, 971 of 1,256 accidental opioid-related deaths (77.3%) against 2,604 of 4,619 matched controls (56.4%) with a benzodiazepine dispensed in the prior 120 days (Gomes et al., 2017; descriptive, no adjusted estimate).

evidence.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Trends in Alcohol and Benzodiazepine Co-involvement, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 1 (image)
evidence.extracted: Of 399,230 US opioid-involved poisoning deaths in 1999–2017, the share whose death certificates also named benzodiazepines rose from 8.7% in 1999 to 26.2% in 2010 and fell to 21.0% in 2017; death rates for opioid overdoses involving benzodiazepines rose 10.3-fold, against 5.0-fold for all opioid overdose deaths. By subtype: heroin 4.0% (1999) to 17.1% (2017); methadone 15.6% (2000) to 32.0% (2017); prescription opioids 15.6% (2000) to 33.1% (2017); synthetic opioids between 15.0% and 25.9%.

evidence.extracted: 2015–2017: 26,728 of 122,940 opioid overdose deaths (21.7%) named benzodiazepines; men 15,837 of 82,506 (19.2%), women 10,891 of 40,434 (26.9%); heroin 6,972 of 43,940 (15.9%); methadone 3,202 of 9,868 (32.4%); prescription opioids 13,905 of 41,709 (33.3%); synthetic opioids 9,978 of 57,459 (17.4%); by state from 5.4% (Delaware) to 45.5% (Arkansas), median 22.0%.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 6th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Death certificates misclassify and omit drugs: about 20% of drug poisoning deaths in 2011 and 12% in 2017 named no specific drug, and states named at least one drug in 54.7% to 99.3% of deaths in 2017; medical-examiner guidance from 2013 recommends benzodiazepine testing; the database has no individual-level data, so deaths involving opioids, benzodiazepines and alcohol together cannot be counted. The authors note two toxicology studies with benzodiazepines in 60% of opioid deaths, which they call inconsistent with their data.

evidence.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Unadjusted rates of death from drug overdose, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Of 2,400 US veterans who died of a drug overdose (any drug, any intent) while receiving VHA opioid analgesics in 2004–2009, 1,185 (49%) died during a period of concurrent benzodiazepine prescription, 421 after a benzodiazepine prescription had ended and 794 with none.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, past medication use (120 days), benzodiazepines row
evidence.extracted: Among Ontario public-drug-plan opioid recipients, 971 of 1,256 people who died an accidental, coroner-confirmed opioid-related death (77.3%) and 2,604 of 4,619 matched controls (56.4%) had a benzodiazepine dispensed in the 120 days before the index date (standardized difference 0.46); this is a descriptive comparison after matching, and no adjusted estimate for benzodiazepines is reported.

risk_of_bias.note: Measurement could change the figures materially: certificate mentions depend on toxicology and reporting that vary by state and year (12–20% of drug poisoning deaths with no drug named), and prescription records do not show that the medicine was taken.

inconsistency.note: The figures differ (21% on certificates; 49% and 77% with prescriptions) because they measure different things; all agree that benzodiazepines are common in opioid deaths.

indirectness.note: None as worded: each source's measure and population is stated.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (METHODS §6.3): it starts low and is never upgraded for size. Risk of bias −1 for measurement: death certificates under-record drugs and testing practices changed over the period, so the certificate shares are floors and their trend partly reflects reporting; the prescription-based shares come from two selected populations (VHA veterans; Ontario public-drug-plan recipients) and record dispensing, not use. Inconsistency 0 (the measures differ, the conclusion does not), indirectness 0 as worded, imprecision 0. Certainty very low for the exact shares; that benzodiazepines appear in a substantial minority to a majority of opioid deaths, depending on the measure, is consistent across three independent sources (status: replicated). The claim deliberately says nothing about risk, which is the subject of the answer on prescribed benzodiazepines with opioids.

verification.flag_note: A toxicology-based national source (for example CDC SUDORS, report R3 in the interactions DOI list) would give a less under-recorded figure; Gladden et al. 2019 (MMWR, 10.15585/mmwr.mm6834a2) covers 2017–2018.
